note.en: Indra for the Devas and Virochana for the Asuras come as fellow pupils to Prajapati and study together for thirty-two years.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh Khanda - 'Indra went from the Devas, Virokana from the Asuras, and both, without having communicated with each other, approached Pragapati, holding fuel in their hands, as is the custom for pupils approaching their master'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 7, 2-3 has Indra and Virochana approach Prajapati together as fellow pupils and dwell there thirty-two years.

note.en: Virochana takes the body to be the Self and teaches that doctrine to the Asuras, which the Upanishad marks as the doctrine that perishes.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Eighth Khanda - 'Virokana, satisfied in his heart, went to the Asuras and preached that doctrine to them, that the self (the body) alone is to be worshipped'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 8, 4 has Virochana carry away the mistaken teaching that the body is the Self and preach it to the Asuras.

note.en: Unlike Virochana, Indra sees that a self identified with the body perishes with it, and returns for further teaching on the true Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Ninth Khanda - 'Taking fuel in his hand he came again as a pupil to Pragapati' after seeing that the bodily self 'will perish in fact as soon as the body perishes'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 9, 1-3 has Indra alone detect the flaw in the bodily self and return as a pupil for further instruction on the Self.

note.en: The instruction Indra pursues through successive stays with Prajapati is the identification of the Self with Brahman.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh Khanda - Pragapati: 'The person that is seen in the eye, that is the Self. This is what I have said. This is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 7, 4 records the teaching identifying the Self with Brahman that Indra receives from Prajapati.

note.en: Indra is the central pupil of the Chandogya's longest instruction sequence, returning repeatedly until the true Self is taught.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh to Ninth Khandas - Prajapati tells Indra 'Live with me another thirty-two years'

verification.notes: Indra appears across Chandogya VIII, 7-9 as the persistent pupil in the Prajapati instruction cycle.

note.en: Virochana's only Upanishadic role is as the Asura pupil who departs satisfied with an incomplete answer.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh and Eighth Khandas - 'Virokana from the Asuras' approaches Pragapati and departs 'satisfied in his heart'

verification.notes: Virochana appears in Chandogya VIII, 7-8 as Indra's Asura counterpart in the Prajapati episode.

note.en: Narada approaches Sanatkumara as a pupil, and the whole seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya is the instruction that follows.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'Narada approached Sanatkumara and said, Teach me, Sir!'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 1, 1 opens with Narada formally approaching Sanatkumara for instruction, and VII, 26, 2 closes with Sanatkumara showing him the other side of darkness.

note.en: The closing sentence of the Chandogya's seventh Prapathaka names the teaching as completed from Sanatkumara to Narada.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, Twenty-sixth Khanda - 'The venerable Sanatkumara showed to Narada, after his faults had been rubbed out, the other side of darkness'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 26, 2 states the completed transmission from Sanatkumara to Narada.

note.en: Narada's request is framed as the insufficiency of textual learning without knowledge of the Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First Khanda - Narada: 'But, Sir, with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 1, 3 has Narada confess that his mastery of the Vedas has not given him knowledge of the Self.

note.en: Narada is the questioner whose successive requests for something better drive the whole of Chandogya VII.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First to Twenty-sixth Khandas - Narada as the questioner throughout, asking 'Sir, is there something better than a name?'

verification.notes: Narada is the named interlocutor of the entire seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya Upanishad.

note.en: Sanatkumara is the teacher of Chandogya VII, whom the text's closing line identifies with Skanda.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, Twenty-sixth Khanda - 'They call Sanatkumara Skanda, yea, Skanda they call him'

verification.notes: Sanatkumara is the teacher of the whole seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya and is identified there with Skanda.

note.en: Uddalaka Aruni is the father-teacher of the Chandogya's sixth Prapathaka.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'To him his father (Uddalaka, the son of Aruna) said: Svetaketu, go to school'

verification.notes: Aruni, that is Uddalaka Aruni, is the teaching father of Chandogya VI and appears again in the Kaushitaki and Brihadaranyaka.

note.en: Aruni's opening question to his son sets out the knowledge of the one by which all else is known.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'have you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what cannot be heard, by which we perceive what cannot be perceived, by which we know what cannot be known?'

verification.notes: Chandogya VI, 1, 3 has Uddalaka Aruni pose the question that opens his teaching on the one reality by which all is known.

note.en: Aruni teaches the Self through sleep, hunger and thirst as successive demonstrations of the one True.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, Eighth Khanda - 'Uddalaka Aruni said to his son Svetaketu: Learn from me the true nature of sleep (svapna). When a man sleeps here, then, my dear son, he becomes united with the True'

verification.notes: Chandogya VI, 8, 1 has Uddalaka Aruni teach that in sleep a man goes to his own Self.

note.en: The Kaushitaki opens with Aruni deputing his son to a sacrifice, then taking fuel in hand and coming to Chitra Gangyayani as a pupil himself.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, First Adhyaya - 'Kitra Gangyayani, forsooth, wishing to perform a sacrifice, chose Aruni (Uddalaka, to be his chief priest). But Aruni sent his son, Svetaketu'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki I, 1 opens with Aruni chosen as chief priest, sending his son in his place, and then himself coming to Chitra as a pupil with fuel in hand.

note.en: Yama's first boon names Nachiketa's father as Auddalaki Aruni; at Katha I, 1, 1 the same father is called Vajasravasa.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Yama: 'Through my favour Auddalaki Aruni, thy father, will know thee, and be again towards thee as he was before'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 11 names Nachiketa's father as Auddalaki Aruni in Yama's granting of the first boon.

note.en: Nachiketa's first boon is his father's goodwill; Yama identifies the father as Auddalaki Aruni.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Nachiketa: 'I choose that Gautama, my father, be pacified, kind, and free from anger towards me'; Yama names him 'Auddalaki Aruni, thy father'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 10-11 has Nachiketa ask for his father's goodwill and Yama name that father Auddalaki Aruni.

note.en: Yama grants Nachiketa three boons after his three-night wait, and the third boon is the teaching on what survives death.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Yama: 'O Brahmana, as thou, a venerable guest, hast dwelt in my house three nights without eating, therefore choose now three boons'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 9 begins the instruction in which Yama grants Nachiketa three boons and teaches him what follows death.

note.en: Nachiketa is the pupil of Death himself, refusing wealth and long life in favour of the question of the Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Nachiketa asks his boons of Death, saying 'What will be the work of Yama... which to-day he has to do unto me?'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 5-11 has Nachiketa enter Yama's abode and receive instruction from him as his pupil.

note.en: Nachiketa is the boy whose faith and refusal of lesser boons frames the entire Katha Upanishad.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - 'faith entered into the heart of Nakiketas, who was still a boy'

verification.notes: Nachiketa is the named pupil of the whole Katha Upanishad, introduced at Katha I, 1, 2.

note.en: Nachiketa's questioning of Death moves from the heavenly world to the Self that death does not touch.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - 'In the heaven-world there is no fear; thou art not there, O Death, and no one is afraid on account of old age'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 12 has Nachiketa press Yama past the fire-sacrifice toward what remains when the body dies.

note.en: Indra makes his own self-knowledge the boon he grants Pratardana, and teaches him prana as the conscious self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - Indra: 'Know me only; that is what I deem most beneficial for man, that he should know me'; and 'I am prana, meditate on me as the conscious self'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki III, 1-2 has Indra instruct Pratardana son of Divodasa on prana as the conscious self.

note.en: Pratardana asks Indra to choose the boon for him, and receives instruction rather than a gift.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - 'Pratardana, forsooth, the son of Divodasa (king of Kasi), came by means of fighting and strength to the beloved abode of Indra'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki III, 1 has Pratardana reach Indra's abode and receive instruction in place of an ordinary boon.

note.en: Pratardana is the royal interlocutor of the Kaushitaki's third Adhyaya on prana.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - Pratardana as Indra's interlocutor, objecting that 'the pranas become one'

verification.notes: Pratardana is the named questioner of the third Adhyaya of the Kaushitaki Upanishad.

note.en: Varuna teaches his son Bhrigu by sending him repeatedly to perform penance until he perceives that bliss is Brahman.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli (the Chapter of Bhrigu), First Anuvaka - 'Bhrigu Varuni went to his father Varuna, saying: Sir, teach me Brahman.' He told him this, viz. Food, breath, the eye, the ear, mind, speech'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 1 has Bhrigu approach his father Varuna for instruction in Brahman and receive the successive definitions of it.

note.en: Bhrigu asks his father for the knowledge of Brahman and is told to seek out that from which beings are born.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli (the Chapter of Bhrigu), First Anuvaka - 'Bhrigu Varuni went to his father Varuna, saying: Sir, teach me Brahman'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 1 has Bhrigu formally request instruction in Brahman from Varuna.

note.en: The Taittiriya calls him Bhrigu Varuni and states directly that he went to his father Varuna.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli, First Anuvaka - 'Bhrigu Varuni went to his father Varuna'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 1 names Varuna as Bhrigu's father, the patronymic Varuni carrying the same descent.

note.en: In the Taittiriya the teaching of Brahman passes from Varuna to his son Bhrigu.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli, First Anuvaka - 'Bhrigu Varuni went to his father Varuna'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 1 states the father-son relation between Varuna and Bhrigu.

note.en: The Bhrigu Valli ends with the doctrine that bliss is Brahman, named as the joint knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuna.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli, Sixth Anuvaka - 'He perceived that bliss is Brahman... This is the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuna, exalted in the highest heaven'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 6 names the completed doctrine the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuna.

note.en: Varuna is named alongside his son as holder of the Taittiriya's concluding knowledge of Brahman as bliss.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli, Sixth Anuvaka - 'This is the knowledge of Bhrigu and Varuna, exalted in the highest heaven (in the heart)'

verification.notes: Taittiriya III, 6 attributes the concluding knowledge of Brahman jointly to Varuna and Bhrigu.

note.en: The Taittiriya's third chapter is called the Bhrigu Valli and is built entirely around his instruction.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli, titled 'THE CHAPTER OF BHRIGU' - 'Bhrigu Varuni went to his father Varuna'

verification.notes: The third Valli of the Taittiriya Upanishad is named the Bhrigu Valli after its pupil.

note.en: Varuna appears in the Upanishads chiefly as the father who teaches Bhrigu the nature of Brahman.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Taittiriya Upanishad, Third Valli - Varuna as the instructing father throughout the Bhrigu Valli

verification.notes: Varuna is the teacher of the whole third Valli of the Taittiriya Upanishad.

note.en: Janaka Vaideha is the royal interlocutor of the Brihadaranyaka's fourth Adhyaya, the longest sustained dialogue in the Upanishad.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Fourth Adhyaya, First Brahmana - 'When Ganaka Vaideha was sitting (to give audience), Yagnavalkya approached, and Ganaka Vaideha said: Yagnavalkya, for what object did you come, wishing for cattle, or for subtle questions?'

verification.notes: Brihadaranyaka IV, 1, 1 opens the Janaka Vaideha dialogues that run through the fourth Adhyaya.

note.en: Janaka collects definitions of Brahman from many teachers and brings each in turn to be completed.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Fourth Adhyaya, First Brahmana - Ganaka Vaideha: 'Gitvan Sailini told me that speech (vak) is Brahman'; Yagnavalkya: 'this (Brahman) stands on one leg only'

verification.notes: Brihadaranyaka IV, 1 has Janaka recite the partial definitions of Brahman he has been given by earlier teachers, each of which is then completed.

note.en: Janaka's question 'Who is that Self?' opens the Brihadaranyaka's central teaching on the self-luminous person.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Fourth Adhyaya, Third Brahmana - Ganaka Vaideha: 'Who is that Self?' Yagnavalkya replied: 'He who is within the heart, surrounded by the Pranas (senses), the person of light, consisting of knowledge'

verification.notes: Brihadaranyaka IV, 3, 7 has Janaka ask directly after the Self and receive the teaching of the person of light within the heart.

note.en: Janaka's surrender of the Videhas to his teacher confirms his kingship over them in the Upanishad.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Fourth Adhyaya, Second Brahmana - 'Here are the Videhas, and here am I (thy slave)', said by Ganaka Vaideha

verification.notes: Brihadaranyaka IV, 2, 4 confirms Janaka's rule over the Videhas in his own words.

note.en: Janaka is declared to have reached fearlessness, the Upanishad's term for the condition beyond death and rebirth.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Fourth Adhyaya, Second Brahmana - 'O Ganaka, you have indeed reached fearlessness,--thus said Yagnavalkya. Then Ganaka said: May that fearlessness come to you also'

verification.notes: Brihadaranyaka IV, 2, 4 declares Janaka to have reached the fearlessness that the teaching confers.

note.en: Bharadvaja is named several times in the Brihadaranyaka vamsa as a teacher from whom the doctrine was received.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Second Adhyaya, Sixth Brahmana (the Vamsa or line of teachers) - '15. Parasarya from Bharadvaja, 16. Bharadvaja from Bharadvaja and Gautama, 17. Gautama from Bharadvaja'

verification.notes: The Brihadaranyaka's closing line of teachers names Bharadvaja repeatedly as a link in the transmission of the Madhukanda.

note.en: Vali's strength as leader of the woodland hosts is traced to his father Indra.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'Bali, the woodland hosts who led... Was Indra's child'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI states Vali's descent from Indra.

note.en: Sugriva is twice named in this canto as the offspring of the Sun.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'The Sun, was great Sugriva's sire'; and later 'Sugriva, offspring of the Sun'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI states Sugriva's descent from Surya twice in the same canto.

note.en: Nila's fiery character in the war books is grounded in his descent from Agni.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'From Agni, Nila bright as flame'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI states Nila's descent from Agni.

note.en: Sushena, the senior Vanara commander, is begotten by Varuna.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'Varun was father of Sushen'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI names Varuna as Sushena's father in the Vanara roll.

note.en: Sushena's parentage from Varuna is given in the canto that creates the Vanara host.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'Varun was father of Sushen'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI states Sushena's descent from Varuna.

note.en: Dwivida is always named beside Mainda, the two being sons of the Ashvin twins.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'Dwivida and Mainda named, For beauty like their sires were famed'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI pairs Dwivida and Mainda as sons of the Ashvins.

note.en: The whole Vanara host, Hanuman included, is created at Brahma's command to aid the incarnate Vishnu.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'The self-existent Lord of all Addressed the Gods... Make helps, in war to lend him aid, In forms that change at will, arrayed'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI has Brahma command the gods to beget the Vanara host, Hanuman among them, as helpers for Vishnu's incarnation.

note.en: Vali's begetting by Indra happens in obedience to Brahma's command to create helpers for Vishnu.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'Thus by the mighty Sire addressed They all obeyed his high behest, And thus begot in countless swarms Brave sons disguised in sylvan forms'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI frames every Vanara chief, Vali included, as begotten on Brahma's instruction.

note.en: Griffith names Vali and Sugriva the two brothers at the head of the Vanara host.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XVI: The Vanars - 'The leaders of the monkey band By the two brothers took their stand, Sugriva, offspring of the Sun, And Bali, Indra's mighty one'

verification.notes: Bala Kanda XVI calls Vali and Sugriva the two brothers who lead the monkey band.

note.en: Jatayus names Sampati as his elder brother, both being sons of Arun.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book III (Aranya Kanda), Canto XIV: Jatayus - 'And sons of Arun red as morn Sampati first, then I was born, Me then, O tamer of the foe, Jatayus, son of S'yeni, know'

verification.notes: Aranya Kanda XIV has Jatayus himself declare that he and Sampati are both sons of Arun, Sampati the elder.

note.en: Sampati is the elder of the two vulture brothers born of Arun.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book III (Aranya Kanda), Canto XIV: Jatayus - 'sons of Arun red as morn Sampati first, then I was born'

verification.notes: Aranya Kanda XIV establishes Sampati as Jatayus' elder brother.

note.en: Jatayus is Dasharatha's old friend, which is why he offers to guard Rama's household in the forest.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book III (Aranya Kanda), Canto XIV: Jatayus - 'In me, dear sons, the friend behold Your royal father loved of old'; and 'He often in the days gone by Had heard his father tell How, linked with him in friendship's tie, He loved Jatayus well'

verification.notes: Aranya Kanda XIV has Jatayus present himself as Dasharatha's old friend, which Rama confirms from his father's own account.

note.en: Jatayus undertakes to guard Sita whenever Rama and Lakshmana are away, the pledge that leads to his death.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book III (Aranya Kanda), Canto XIV: Jatayus - 'Thy ready helper will I be, And guard thy house, if thou agree: When thou and Lakshman urge the chase By Sita's side shall be my place'

verification.notes: Aranya Kanda XIV records Jatayus' offer to guard Sita while Rama and Lakshmana hunt, which Rama accepts with an embrace.

note.en: Jambavan is the Vanara who puts the decisive question to Sampati about where Sita is held.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book IV (Kishkindha Kanda), Canto LIX: Sampati's Story - 'And Jambavan with joyous breast The vulture king again addressed: Where, where is Sita?'

verification.notes: Kishkindha LIX has Jambavan question Sampati directly about Sita's whereabouts.

note.en: Sampati's report of his son's sighting fixes Sita's prison in the south and sends Hanuman across the ocean.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book IV (Kishkindha Kanda), Canto LIX: Sampati's Story - 'Now listen, and my words shall show What of the Maithil dame I know, And in what distant prison lies The lady of the long dark eyes'

verification.notes: Kishkindha LIX has Sampati report, from his son Suparshva's sighting, that Sita was carried south by a giant.

note.en: Sampati is the witness, at one remove, who identifies Ravana as Sita's captor and the south as his course.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Book IV (Kishkindha Kanda), Canto LIX: Sampati's Story - Suparshva's report: 'Before mine eyes a giant flew Whose monstrous form was dark of hue And struggling in his grasp was borne A lady radiant as the morn. Swift to the south his course he bent'

verification.notes: Kishkindha LIX relays, through Sampati, the sighting of Ravana carrying Sita southward, the saints naming the robber.
